claims.text: Phase stability in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys is governed by the balance between atomic size misfit and configurational entropy.
Atomic size misfit promotes lattice strain.
Atomic size misfit promotes formation of bcc or intermetallic phases.
Configurational entropy stabilizes the fcc phase.
An optimal balance of atomic size misfit and configurational entropy enables retention of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
The baseline Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy exhibits a mixture of fcc and bcc phases.
Varying Al content modulates atomic size misfit.
Atomic size misfit governs the fcc-to-bcc/intermetallic phase balance through lattice distortion.
Increasing Al concentration enhances atomic size misfit.
The lattice strain induced by increasing Al favors bcc or intermetallic phase formation.
Formation of bcc or intermetallic phases may compromise mechanical and chemical properties.
At elevated temperatures, configurational entropy can stabilize fcc if atomic size misfit remains below a critical threshold.
An optimal Al concentration will produce a predominantly fcc matrix at high temperature.
A predominantly fcc matrix at high temperature will ensure high-temperature strength and radiation tolerance.
An optimal composition will exhibit a reversible or controlled presence of bcc or secondary phases at cryogenic temperatures.
The presence of bcc or secondary phases at cryogenic temperatures will enable cryogenic toughness.
Departures from the optimal composition will cause excessive intermetallic formation.
Excessive intermetallic formation will compromise strength, environmental resistance, and toughness.
The mid-range mixed-fcc/bcc baseline has moderate performance under temperature extremes and environmental exposure.
Direct quantitative evidence linking atomic size misfit to exact phase balance and property performance in this alloy system is currently lacking.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says bcc or intermetallic formation may compromise mechanical properties, whereas the predicted outcome says controlled bcc or secondary-phase formation enables cryogenic toughness. The distinction between beneficial and detrimental phase fractions, morphologies, or phase types is not defined.

The hypothesis broadly associates configurational entropy with fcc stabilization, but the predicted outcome also requires temperature-dependent appearance of bcc or secondary phases at cryogenic temperature without explaining whether this transformation is thermodynamically reversible or kinetically accessible.
